newsitem.title: FRANCE: South Korea set on OECD entry, but trouble at home.
newsitem.headline: South Korea set on OECD entry, but trouble at home.

text.p: South Korean Foreign Minister Gong Ro-Myung said on Friday he was confident of winning a parliamentary vote on joining the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) despite stiff opposition party resistance.
"It is true there are some views in Korea, particularly in the opposition, that the time for accession is not particularly appropriate," Gong told a news conference at the OECD here.

Even if the economy was slowing down after a sustained period of strong growth, it was time that South Korea was accepted in the OECD, he said after a ceremony to mark the invitation for Seoul to become the second Asian member.

"I am pretty confident we can have the accession concurred," Gong he said when asked if the government, which has a narrow majority in parliament, was certain of overcoming opposition when a vote is taken in December.
He faces resistance from opposition groups that warn the OECD could force South Korea to pry its local markets open to offshore competition more rapidly.
Gong said South Korea had been transformed from one of the world's poorest economies before an industrialisation drive in the 1960s and now had the 11th highest output in the world.
"Entry into the OECD is not our final goal, but a starting point for further liberalisation of the economy," he said.

Asked about South Korea's progress in opening its economy, OECD secretary general Donald Johnson said: "One of the major benefits is peer group pressure, constantly pushing you to move further and further down the path of liberalisation. Korea has made the commitment".
Gong said Seoul would raise limits on foreign investment by outsiders in firms to 20 percent in 1996 and 23 percent in 1997.

A major lobby group, the Citizens Coalition for Economic Justice, has promised a nationwide campaign against membership of the OECD, a research and debating forum which is spreading its message of free-market economics beyond the traditional reserve of the richest industrialised nations.
South Korea would expand OECD membership to 29 on the heels of Poland and give it a greater weight in Asia, where long-time member Japan has been the only Asian member to date.
